implementation_notes: The portable JPA route: an AttributeConverter serializes the graph with Jackson (or another JSON library) into a String or byte[] attribute, optionally annotated @Lob so the provider picks CLOB/BLOB, and the converter is the pattern's mapper. It works on any JPA provider and any column type, but the graph is invisible to JPQL, so it cannot be queried or indexed without native SQL or a JSON-capable provider.
pitfalls: @Lob on a String attribute is a classic trap: some providers map it to a database large-object handle instead of text, so the value is unreadable outside the owning session - check the physical column type.
The converter runs on every dirty check: returning a fresh object each call forces the entity to look dirty on every flush unless equality is stable or the attribute is replaced as a whole.
Silent field drift: without FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES configuration a renamed property quietly drops data on the next write.

variants.name: JPA AttributeConverter + JSON library into a CLOB

variants.name: Hibernate 6 native JSON mapping
variants.implementation_notes: Hibernate 6 maps an arbitrary attribute to a database JSON/JSONB column: @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) selects the JSON JDBC type and Hibernate detects the JSON library (Jackson, Gson, JSON-B) for conversion. The payload stays reachable from native SQL/JSON functions, which is the reason to prefer this variant over a converter-managed CLOB; it requires Hibernate 6 plus a database with a JSON type.
pitfalls: Without an explicit @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) Hibernate does not use the JSON type at all, and the attribute silently degrades to an ordinary basic mapping.
Dirty checking compares the serialized form, so in-place mutation of the graph may not be detected unless the attribute is reassigned or bytecode enhancement is in play.

variants.name: Legacy java.io.Serializable blob
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-JSON classic: the graph implements java.io.Serializable and an ObjectOutputStream writes it into a @Lob byte[] attribute. Keep it only for data you already hold; new designs should not adopt it because the format binds payloads to exact class names and serialVersionUIDs, breaks on refactoring and makes deserialization of untrusted bytes a well-known remote-code-execution vector (mitigate with ObjectInputFilter when legacy data must still be read).
pitfalls: Renaming a class, moving a package or changing serialVersionUID makes stored blobs throw InvalidClassException, turning a code refactoring into a data migration.
ObjectInputStream instantiates whatever the stream names, so legacy blobs must be treated as untrusted input and filtered with an ObjectInputFilter allow-list.
